...And getting trolled when he decides to spam Itemfinder everywhere until I behave.

Cass joined us late in E18.
Originally she was going to be an animator!

But she more than made up for it in ways I already basically gushed about in another section, so I'll spare her here.
She did suggest we take on a certain Toothpastefairy, or Perry!
He happened to be working on some mods anyway so we picked him up to help out and he's just been fantastic for the whole tail end of the ride.
I'm very grateful for him helping us out with programming reliably, and also being totally down to enable whatever bullshit Cass or I get up to.
He's done a lot of quality-of-life improvements for y'all especially, such as that quick TM view in the bag!
Other late-joining stars include The Legendary Crim.
You might know of them from their work on literally every other fangame in existence.
It's been a huge help to have a second spriter and mapper on the team.
Even though they were originally just learning both when I asked them to help with Starlight, they learn fast and caught up quick.
There's no way we could've made some of the postgame content as gorgeous as it has been without them.
Last but not least, we also acquired an Azzie!
Fans might know her from her Tourmaline Travels story, and if not, they might be interested in reading it!
She's helped out with a lot of the sundry postgame dialogue, especially in the Nightclub.
If I had to do it all myself I probably would've gone insane and run into the hills screaming...
...Is that everyone?
I think so...
Gosh, I've written too much already. Let's be done.
But please appreciate everyone who's helped us make it to this point, ne?

AME: This might've been unclear, but to be clear this section is just sort of advice/lessons I've learned in the realm of game development.
There's a handful of things I wish I'd done differently, and so I hope others can learn from my mistakes.
If you're not interested, just hold X or whatever.
Let's start with something positive.
#1: Jack of all trades, master of none...
The lesser-known phrase continues "But better than being a master of one."
Ultimately, I think that is true.
Especially as an indie dev starting out, it's important to be willing to handle all parts of the project yourself.
I pride myself on being able to do it all-- music, writing, programming (eventually...), spriting, mapping, animation, sfx, etc...
The flexibility to do all of that has been a great asset in terms of having confidence in knowing that I could finish this game no matter what.
If you're just starting out, it'll also go a long way to helping you work with team members in a way that works for them, which itself helps build trust.
...So that's great,
However,
I think I've caused myself a lot of problems by relying on that too much.
Good to have the option, but it's equally important to be open to accepting help and letting others take the wheel.
Having explored so many different avenues of development, I quite clearly see what I need to do and practice in order to improve at each of them,
But because I am doing so many things at once, I will not be able to pursue those paths to the ends of quality I'd like.
Frustrating.
It also means I'm prone to taking on too much work myself and overwhelming myself, where I see other teams function better when the lead just
Doesn't Worry About It because it's #NotTheirDepartment.
Pros and cons, I guess.
I wish I'd navigated that a bit better and learned to lean on others more.
Speaking of working with others, we only started using git in the last year of development.
#2: Get git.
No one told me about it before, and if they had, we couldn't work it meaningfully without exported scripts.
But if you're on a team, I can't stress how critical it will be to let them access the project directly.
Save yourself.
It's intimidating to learn at first, but so worth it.
Frankly, that goes for programming itself.
I didn't touch the scripts in Reborn for years and then I was like 'oh this is just rpg maker eventing lmao'
Eventing also intimidating?
Again, if 11-year-old me can do it, so can you.
Okay, what else?
#3: Mind your scope.
Pretty sure every single indie dev advice article will tell you this too, but I sure didn't listen, so I'm repeating it.
Don't make a giant sprawling epic with 18 badges and every legendary in postgame for your first major project.
...It was my second major project, so I'm vindicated.
...But probably just don't do it, like seriously, small goals are best, I p r o m i s e.
It's very easy to underestimate how long everything will take if you're doing it well.
Never doing a game this long again, i s2g.
probably.
#4: Listen to your heart and body.
Okay, I phrased that a little too new-age-spiritually, but, like...
Now that I'm on the other side of a ten year long project, I'm a lot Better at everything,
And yet there are still things I feel like I could learn from my younger self.
One of those things is to let myself rest when I don't feel like working, rather than forcing myself.
I talked a bit about the consequences of this in another dialogue option...
But I very much grew up admiring people with an unhealthy work ethic...
The kind of people who like work until they literally pass out or get sick--
I felt like by not living up to the same standard, or by taking breaks, I was being lazy.
No, that's stupid.
There's something to be said for the programming addage of "work smarter, not harder,"
But more importantly...
Many people are hard on themselves for "being lazy" or "procrastinating" but we are humans who need rest.
Listening to yourself when you don't want to work, or when you need to relax, and choosing to trust yourself,
That's a necessary habit if you want to be in it for the long term.
Seriously, I don't want anyone to go through what I have.
#5, last one: Have fun.
Listen, I know this sounds hokey, but I -promise- this is tangible real advice.
I just said that working harder and forcing yourself is bad, right?
So what's the trick to get good at something if you're not feeling it?
It's still to do it a lot, but the hack there is to -want- to do it a lot.
If you're having fun, you're going to want to do it a lot, and you'll naturally get good at it.
See?
And especially with long-haul development projects, like...
You either find a way to make it fun for yourself, or it's miserable and drags out forever.
I really can't stress this one enough.
Okay, go out there and make some vidya, y'all.

Hi, I'm Vulpes!

Anyway.
Getting involved in Reborn has taught me a lot, and it's been really fun too!
And here's hoping any future projects are even more fun!
So I started helping out with Reborn in 2018.
I was checking a forum thread and Ame mentioned she was looking for another animator.
I really wanted to help with the game, since, well...
Reborn is probably the only reason I'm still interested in Pokémon in general.
I'd been a fan since I was five, maybe earlier, so Pokémon was a pretty big part of my life.
But I started losing interest between BW2 and XY, and drifted away from the franchise by ORAS.
I don't know exactly why, but Reborn brought that interest back.
And I get extremely sentimental over everything, so having such a big part of my life revived like that...
It meant a lot.
Anyway, as I was saying, I really wanted to help out because of that.
But I was also convinced I would be a burden on the team.
I almost talked myself out of applying altogether.
But I'm very glad I didn't.
That choice is probably in the top three decisions I've ever made in my life.
Even so, it took a bit of getting used to.
All my animation experience at the time was in 3D, and the technical stuff didn't carry over.
It wound up with me thinking stuff like "Oh, a spiral will be easy to make!",
And then it would take me a month.
As opposed to like an hour in a 3D program.
Fun fact that is definitely not linked to this in any way:
My least favorite Pokémon is Shiinotic, and my least favorite move is Strength Sap.
But I got better, and eventually even started using 3D to improve my 2D stuff.
Have you seen the Genesis Supernova animation yet?
I made all the unique graphics for that by making a 3D reference pose to get the perspective right.
(I mostly just mentioned it because it's my favorite animation I've made and you should watch it.)
Actually, you know what?
Give me one... second...
There!
I have a team on hand now with some of the animations I made!
Can't have all of them because I made a fair number of Z-Moves,
But this is all I did for the game for like four years, I want to show it off.
But I've been working on other stuff recently too.
I also started helping with the code once we hit testing for the final episode!
I had a little experience before that, but it was in a language that went out of use before I was born.

And to this day I'm still messing up basic syntax.
I'm being dramatic, it's been two months at most, of course I'm not brilliant yet.

VULPES: "But Vulpes," I hear you ask.
Why do you have this option when you said you weren't a people person?
Assuming you read the first option, that is.
The answer is I just want an excuse to get a bunch of stuff off my chest.
And everyone here helped me deal with it, so there.
This is going to get kind of heavy, so here's a chance to back out if you're not up for it.
So, it might seem obvious from my other answers,
But I had pretty bad anxiety since even before I joined the team.
Probably with some moderate depression mixed in for flavor.
I think it's been about five years, but thinking back I showed symptoms much earlier.
It wasn't exactly conductive to having a functional life.
For most of the time I've been on the team, Reborn's been the only real anchor I've had to functionality.
Without the others, I'd have been a lot worse off.
And even now, when I'm starting to get better, they're helping me a lot just by being there.
With most people, I always felt pressured in some way.
Either by how I "should" act around them, or from the expectations they had.
It'd be a lie to say I never felt like that around the others...
But it was a lot less often than with other people.
And even when I did feel like that, after the first couple of months I could deal with it easier.
I wasn't able to actually talk very often, but at the same time I didn't feel guilty or "wrong" for that.
When the whole world tells you "socialise this, network that", even when it's impossible...
Having a space to exist with others, without having to worry about that stuff, was a big comfort.
And it's taken a while, plus some other help, but I'm not as bad now.
I'm able to talk to them without constantly panicking and overthinking.
Even if I'd started recovering without them around, I wouldn't be making nearly as much progress.
Instead of having two or three people I'm comfortable existing around, I have about twelve.
There's only so many things you'll have in common with one person.
But with different people, there's going to be different commonalities.
And it makes it that much easier to talk to them.
And maybe after that, eventually, you'll feel comfortable calling them friends.
And for everyone else on the team?
I think I've finally reached that point.
So really, I owe the others my emotional health and sanity.
And also my existence outside of being the local cryptid.
Still plan on being that IRL though.
Give me a dog or cat over humans any day.
And hey, if any of this resonates with you?
Know that you're probably underestimating yourself as a person.
More people care about you than you think,
And you're much less of a burden than you think.
I got caught up in those thoughts a lot too.
But your brain is lying.
Even if you can't believe me right now, keep it in mind.
And I hope some day you will be able to.
